title: Research
text:
I’m fascinated by flowers and their evolution. Who wouldn’t be? Flowers are beautifully complex and ecologically important organs, and evolution has produced an astonishing diversity of them, on which most terrestrial ecosystems depend. How, when and why did they evolve? What mechanisms and processes drive floral evolution? And how might climate change affect it?
Through my research, I study how flowering plants evolve and respond to changes in their environment. I focus mainly, but not only, on the ecological and evolutionary processes shaping floral and vegetative traits, and on how their evolution is affected by changes in pollinators and abiotic factors, such as those associated with climate change and introduction events. To explore this, I combine field and greenhouse studies to compare the evolvability, phenotypic plasticity and divergence of vegetative and floral traits, including flower morphology and nectar.

title: Research
section: Floral evolution along Andean altitudinal gradients
text:
Floral evolution along Andean altitudinal gradients



  
  
  



Lund University
High-altitude mountain ranges offer steep environmental gradients over short distances, making them natural laboratories for studying adaptation. Studying variation in floral phenotypes along altitudinal gradients, I investigate how floral integration and allometry are shaped by changes in abiotic- and pollinator-mediated selection in Andean communities. Knowing how flowering plants respond to changes in their environment will help us understand how climate change and pollinator decline may affect flower evolution over the next decades.

title: Research
section: Floral evolution under novel pollination environments
text:
Floral evolution under novel pollination environments



  
  
  



University of Sussex
Pollinator declines and changes in the distribution of flowering plants are reshaping their selective environment. During my PhD, I explored the plasticity, evolvability and local adaptation of floral traits under novel pollination environments. Using native and naturalised populations of Digitalis purpurea, I combined common-garden, transplant and resurrection experiments with genomic and multivariate analyses to show how nectar and floral morphology differ in their evolutionary potential, and how this can affect their evolution when they encounter new pollinators after introduction events.

title: Research
section: Thermal plasticity and rapid evolution under climate change
text:
Thermal plasticity and rapid evolution under climate change



  
  
  



University of Sussex / University of Helsinki
Rising temperatures are imposing new selection pressures on plants worldwide, which must adjust their vegetative and reproductive traits to persist. But do plants survive through plasticity, genetic change, or both? Using a resurrection approach, I compare how ancestral and descendant plants cope with increasing temperatures. Combining greenhouse and transplant experiments across the native range of Hypericum perforatum, I study thermal plasticity, recent phenotypic divergence and current natural selection on vegetative and floral traits.

title: Research
section: Polyploidy and floral divergence in specialised pollination systems
text:
Polyploidy and floral divergence in specialised pollination systems



  
  
    
    © Paul G. Johnson, iNaturalist, CC BY-NC-SA
  
  



Lund University
Whole-genome duplication is a major driver of plant diversification. The perennial herb Lithophragma bolanderi comprises diploid, tetraploid and hexaploid populations, with polyploids having originated through repeated autopolyploidization. This species coevolves with its specialised pollinators, Greya moths, with which it forms a nursery pollination system. As part of this project, I combine range-wide sampling, common-garden and crossing experiments, genomics and field surveys to study how polyploidy shapes floral morphology and plant–pollinator interactions. Ongoing work explores how polyploids overcome reproductive isolation from their ancestors and establish despite the minority cytotype disadvantage.



See my publications for more.

title: Andrés Romero Bravo
text:
Andres Romero Bravo
    Plant evolutionary ecologist
    ¡Hola! I am Andrés. I am originally from Madrid (Spain), where I lived most of my life and started my higher education with a degree in Teaching and a degree in Biology. My academic career has taken me to live in places like Torres del Paine (Chile), Lund (Sweden), where I obtained a MSc in Plant Science, and Lewes (UK), where I studied my PhD. I have recently returned to Lund to continue my career as a postdoctoral researcher.
    I am fascinated by floral evolution and plant–pollinator interactions and I study the ecological and evolutionary processes that affect the responses of flowering plants to environmental change. In my research, I combine quantitative genetics, phenotypic plasticity, and field and greenhouse experiments to understand how reproductive and vegetative traits respond to changes in abiotic and biotic environments.
    I conducted my PhD at the University of Sussex, within the Plant Evolutionary Ecology Lab, investigating floral plasticity, evolvability, and local adaptation under novel pollination environments. My work here combined common-garden, transplant, and resurrection experiments with genomic and multivariate statistical analyses.
    Beyond research, I am a co-founder and Secretary of Jóvenes por la Botánica Española (JxBE), a society for young botanists in Spain focused on connecting young people interested in plants and fighting plant blindness.
    Growing up, and thanks to my parents, I developed an interest in exploring and studying nature. This soon grew into an ever-growing interest in mountaineering, nature photography and science communication. I enjoy making the most of my background in education to bridge academia and the wider public, and in 2018, I started La naturaleza al detalle, a nature photography blog where I use nature photography to share my passion for the natural world with a broad audience.
